doc.title: Oliver Nelson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 10, 2020

chapter: Sound Pieces and Los Angeles studios
title: The studio factory and the timing clock
summary: Coming home exhausted, and the clock and cue sheets used to time television cues to a tenth of a second.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Would he come home and talk about his day?
Come home exhausted sometimes, especially with the television stuff.

He said, “Man I don’t want to hear another note for a long time.” That would last about two days and then he’s — “Well I’m ready to get back.” And everybody needs to get away from that stuff. Because it’s a factory. I mean it literally is a factory. You kind of put this stuff out and you’ve got to do it within a certain timeframe and you’ve got to make sure it’s right. And the technology was so different, Monk, then than it is now. I’m going to see if I can point something to you. I’m going to turn the screen around. If you look, you see that big brown clock up there?

That clock was the clock that he used to write music for Universal, for television. Because what they would do back then was they would give a cue sheet out and the cue sheet was all timed to a tenth of a second. So the Six Million Dollar Man throws this ball at 2 minutes 22 seconds, and the ball goes slow. And he’d have to use that clock to time everything to a tenth of a second. When you went to the soundstage they had a big clock like that too. And what they would do is the music editors would have to use a thing called a streamer. So they’d scratch the film, because you had this big, big movie screen there and that would tell him when the music started and it would tell him when the music had to stop. So he had to use that clock to be able to write that stuff.
Wow. And I bet you wouldn’t want to be the person in the band who made a real clunker.
